candidate: R1. The AI Act's application dates for high-risk systems were under negotiation

originalSignals.title: Digital Omnibus on AI [EU Legislation in Progress]

summary.text: A European Parliamentary Research Service briefing describes the Commission's proposal of 19 November 2025 to amend the AI Act, part of a wider digital package. The proposal responds to delays in designating national competent authorities and in publishing harmonised standards, and aims to ease implementation and reduce the regulatory burden of the AI Act, including by adjusting when the rules for high-risk AI systems start to apply. The briefing sets out the proposal and the state of the co-legislators' work on it.
summary.label: ai-generated

source.title: Digital Omnibus on AI [EU Legislation in Progress]

originalSignals.label: real

originalSignals.title: Council agrees position to streamline rules on Artificial Intelligence

summary.text: The Council of the EU agreed its negotiating position on the Commission's proposal to streamline the AI Act. The Commission had proposed delaying the high-risk rules by up to 16 months, until it confirms that standards and support tools are available; the Council instead set fixed dates, 2 December 2027 for stand-alone high-risk systems and 2 August 2028 for high-risk systems embedded in products. The Council also added a prohibition on AI-generated non-consensual intimate content and child sexual abuse material, reinstated registration for providers who consider their systems exempt from high-risk classification, reinstated a strict-necessity standard for processing sensitive data for bias detection, and moved the deadline for national AI regulatory sandboxes to 2 December 2027. The presidency was to start negotiations with the European Parliament.
summary.label: ai-generated

source.title: Council agrees position to streamline rules on Artificial Intelligence

originalSignals.label: real

pastJudgement.rationale: We took the noise reading. Our incident-question assistant answers engineers' questions about telemetry; nothing in the Commission proposal or the Council position suggests it counts as a high-risk system. The dates were still a Council negotiating position awaiting talks with Parliament. Following a moving draft would cost four people time without changing what Jakob builds. We will revisit if a customer asks about AI Act duties.
pastJudgement.label: replay

candidate: R2. The GDPR changes proposed in the Digital Omnibus met opposition from the data-protection authorities

originalSignals.title: Digital Omnibus: EDPB and EDPS support simplification and competitiveness while raising key concerns

summary.text: The European Data Protection Board and the European Data Protection Supervisor published a joint opinion on the Commission's Digital Omnibus proposal, which would amend the GDPR. They supported a higher risk threshold and a longer deadline for notifying data breaches to authorities, common templates, and harmonisation of the notion of scientific research. They strongly opposed the proposed change to the definition of personal data, saying it went far beyond a technical amendment, departed from the case law of the Court of Justice and would significantly narrow the concept, and they objected to letting the Commission decide when pseudonymised data stops being personal data. They also recommended changes to the provisions on automated decision-making and on processing for AI systems.
summary.label: ai-generated

source.title: Digital Omnibus: EDPB and EDPS support simplification and competitiveness while raising key concerns

originalSignals.label: real

pastJudgement.rationale: We took the threat reading. Our pitch rests on pseudonymised telemetry still counting as personal data. The Commission proposed narrowing that definition and letting itself decide when pseudonymised data stops being personal; the authorities' strong objection shows the point is contested, not settled. Until the co-legislators decide, Anna will keep sales material from leaning on the current definition alone, and Jakob keeps full removal as an option.
pastJudgement.label: replay

candidate: R3. The Cyber Resilience Act's reporting obligations had a fixed start date and draft guidance

originalSignals.title: Commission publishes for feedback draft guidance to assist companies in applying the Cyber Resilience Act

summary.text: The European Commission published draft guidance on the Cyber Resilience Act and invited feedback until 31 March 2026. The draft covers remote data processing solutions, free and open-source software, the concept of support periods and the interplay with other EU law, with attention to making compliance easier for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. The Commission restated that the Act entered into force on 10 December 2024, that its reporting obligations apply from 11 September 2026 and that its main obligations apply from 11 December 2027.

source.title: Commission publishes for feedback draft guidance to assist companies in applying the Cyber Resilience Act

originalSignals.label: real

pastJudgement.rationale: We took the opportunity reading. The reporting obligations start on 11 September 2026, a fixed date our customers supplying industry can plan against, and the draft guidance pays attention to small firms and remote data processing. Telemetry that helps a customer notice and document an incident is what we already collect. Anna answers the consultation before 31 March; Jakob checks whether our own hosted pipeline falls in scope.

originalSignals.title: EY European Start-up-Barometer für das Jahr 2025

summary.text: EY reported (in German) that start-ups in Austria raised 253 million euros in 2025, 56 per cent less than in 2024, across 148 financing rounds, with an average round of about 2 million euros, far below the averages in Germany and the United Kingdom; Austria fell from 15th to 20th place in Europe by volume.
